plan.text: Here is your plan for Data structures final prep in 45-minute sessions. Your exam is on Wednesday 14 October at 9:00. You have 3 study days and 45 minutes a day. Last year's paper put 30 percent of the marks on Hash tables: from keys to buckets and 27 percent of the marks on Binary heaps, priority queues and heapsort. So you will learn 4 lessons: Arrays vs linked lists: linear containers, Hash tables: from keys to buckets, Binary heaps, priority queues and heapsort and Binary search trees: search, insert and delete. We cut Big-O, Big-Omega and Big-Theta, Complexity classes cheat sheet and Chaining vs open addressing. Big-O, Big-Omega and Big-Theta: Lowest weight at 9% of marks; 3 days allow 4 lessons; complexity analysis touched on within each data structure lesson. Your reviews are dated backwards from the exam, so the last one lands the day before. Every answer was checked against your own files.

clips.text:
Arrays vs linked lists: linear containers.
Your lecture slides give you two ways to store a sequence of values: a dynamic array and a singly linked list. The whole skill of this lesson is knowing which one to reach for. The table below uses the exact operations from slide 14 of your deck.
when you need fast random access by position and most inserts happen at the end. when you insert or delete at the front frequently and rarely need to jump to an arbitrary position.
Your slide 10 shows the append function. Trace what happens when you start with an empty dynamic array of capacity 2 and append the values 10, 20, 30. Initial state: data = [ , ], size = 0, capacity = 2. append(10): size (0) capacity (2) to no copy. data[0] = 10, size becomes 1. Array: [10, ].
append(20): size (1) capacity (2) to no copy. data[1] = 20, size becomes 2. Array: [10, 20]. append(30): size (2) === capacity (2) to full. Allocate bigger = new Array(4) (capacity doubles to 4). Copy: bigger[0]=10, bigger[1]=20. data = bigger, capacity = 4. Then data[2] = 30, size becomes 3. Array: [10, 20, 30, ].
Key point: the third append did O of 1 work for the write plus O of n work for the copy of 2 elements. The copy is the rare, expensive step that makes the amortised argument work.
Your slides give you two containers, and the exam will ask you to pick the right one for the job. The decision comes down to three questions: 1. Do you need to jump to position k? A dynamic array stores elements in one contiguous block (slide 8).
Address of element i = base + i times element size, so reading or writing arr[5] is one multiplication and one memory access: theta of 1. A linked list must walk from the head, following next pointers, until it reaches node k: theta of n.
If the operation is "give me the 1000th element", a dynamic array wins before the loop starts. 2. Where do inserts happen? At the front: A linked list creates a new node and points its next to the old head — that is two pointer assignments, theta of 1.
A dynamic array must shift every existing element right by one slot, which is theta of n. At the end: A dynamic array writes to data[size] and increments size. Only when the array is full does it copy everything into a bigger array (slide 10).
With doubling, that copy is rare enough that the average cost per append is theta of 1 amortised (slide 11). A singly linked list can only append in theta of 1 if you keep a reference to the last node; otherwise you must walk the whole list to find it. In the middle: Both are slow.
The array shifts elements (theta of n). The list must search for the position (theta of n) and then the insert itself is theta of 1. 3. How much memory can you waste? A dynamic array reserves spare capacity that it may never fill — up to half the allocated space with doubling.
A linked list stores one extra reference per element (the next pointer), which is theta of n overhead regardless of how full the list is. Neither is "better" here; the trade-off is which kind of waste your scenario tolerates. Slide 14 of your deck summarises every operation in one table.
The exam question Q4a asks you to reproduce exactly this comparison for (i) access by index, (ii) insertion at the front, and (iii) memory use.
Inserting at the end of a dynamic array is always O of 1 — the slides say so. A single append is O of 1 only when the array still has spare capacity. When the array is full, that one append triggers a copy of all n elements, making that single operation O of n.
The 'amortised O of 1' means that across many appends the average cost is constant, not that every individual append is constant.
Your slide 13 gives the JavaScript code. Trace what happens when you start with an empty list and run: Step 1: pushFront(list, 'B') list.head = new Node('B', null) State: head to Node('B', null).
Step 2: pushFront(list, 'A') list.head = new Node('A', list.head) to new Node('A', Node('B', null)) State: head to Node('A') to Node('B') to null. Step 3: find(list, 'B') Start at head: cur = Node('A'), value is 'A' not equal to 'B', move to cur.next. cur = Node('B'), value is 'B' === 'B', return cur.
The function walked 2 nodes. In general, finding the k-th element from the head walks k nodes: theta of n in the worst case.

Hash tables: from keys to buckets.
You've seen arrays and linked lists store things in a straight line. A hash table throws away the line. It gives every key a number — the bucket — and drops the value into that bucket, so a search becomes one jump instead of a walk.
That is the whole trick, and it is why the dictionary ADT on slide 3 of Lecture 2 lists hash tables as O of 1 average for insert, search and delete. The dictionary ADT has three operations: insert(key, value), search(key), delete(key).
A hash table implements them with an array of m buckets and a hash function that maps a key to an index: index = hash(key) mod m. Slide 4 shows the simplest version: with m = 10 and h(k) = k mod 10, the key 23 lands in bucket 3, 47 in bucket 7, 81 in bucket 1.
If every key lands in its own bucket, search is a single array access. The catch: keys collide. Two different keys can map to the same bucket. The two ways to survive collisions are the two designs you must know for the exam: Separate chaining (slide 9): each bucket holds a linked list.
New entries go to the end of the chain. Load factor can exceed 1. Open addressing (slide 10): every entry lives inside the bucket array itself. On a collision you follow a probe sequence until you find an empty slot. Load factor must stay below 1.
What makes a hash function good (slide 5): deterministic — same key, same index; uniform — spreads keys evenly; fast and uses the whole key. The division method h(k) = k mod m works best when m is prime and not close to a power of 2. Strings use a polynomial hash: h = h · 31 + code(c) for each character.
The load factor alpha = n / m (slide 7) decides how fast operations run. As alpha grows, collisions grow. Open addressing slows down badly as alpha approaches 1 — slide 12 shows unsuccessful search taking 50.5 probes at alpha = 0.90.
That is why tables resize: allocate a bigger table (often double) and re-insert every entry. Java's HashMap resizes when alpha exceeds 0.75. Chaining tolerates alpha between 1 and 3. You already know how to trace a linked list; now you trace where each key lands and what happens when two land in the same place.
Chaining with m = 7, from slide 9. Each bucket holds a chain; new keys go to the end.
Think of a hash table as a coat check in a theatre. The attendant has m numbered hooks. When you hand over your coat, they compute a number from your name (the hash) and hang the coat on that hook. Later you say your name, they recompute the number, walk straight to the hook, and grab your coat.
That is O of 1 — no searching through a pile. When two people get the same hook number, the attendant has two options. Chaining: they put a rail next to the hook and hang both coats on it, one behind the other.
Open addressing: they walk to the next empty hook and put the second coat there — but then when you come back, they have to check the first hook, then the next, then the next, until they find yours. The load factor is how many coats per hook.
If the theatre is nearly empty, the attendant almost always finds the right hook immediately. If it is packed, they spend all night walking down the row of hooks — that is the probe explosion. A real coat check attendant can remember where they put a coat that was moved to a different hook.
A hash table cannot: the probe sequence is deterministic and the only memory is the array itself. Also, real names are not uniformly distributed, which is exactly why hash functions need to be uniform — the coat check does not have that problem.
Trace the linear probing example from slide 11: m = 10, h(k) = k mod 10, insert 89, 18, 49, 58, 69. This is the exact skill Q2b on last year's paper tests. Insert 89. 89 mod 10 = 9. Slot 9 is empty. Insert 18. 18 mod 10 = 8. Slot 8 is empty. Insert 49 — first collision. 49 mod 10 = 9, but slot 9 is taken.
Probe i=1: slot 0 is empty. 2 probes total. Insert 58 — a longer probe. 58 mod 10 = 8, taken. i=1: slot 9 taken. i=2: slot 0 taken. i=3: slot 1 empty. 4 probes. Insert 69. 69 mod 10 = 9, taken. i=1: slot 0 taken. i=2: slot 1 taken. i=3: slot 2 empty. 4 probes.
A good hash function just needs to be fast to compute — any function that turns a key into a number will do. Slide 5 requires a good hash function to be uniform — spread keys evenly over the buckets.
If h(k) = k mod 10 and all your keys end in 0, every key lands in bucket 0 and the table degrades to a single linked list: O of n search. A fast hash that ignores most buckets is worse than a slower one that spreads keys out.
Insert 50, 700, 76, 85, 92, 73, 101 into a table with m = 7, h(k) = k mod 7. New entries go to the end of the chain. 50 mod 7 = 1 to bucket 1: [50]. 700 mod 7 = 0 to bucket 0: [700]. 76 mod 7 = 6 to bucket 6: [76]. 85 mod 7 = 1 to bucket 1: [50, 85]. 92 mod 7 = 1 to bucket 1: [50, 85, 92].
73 mod 7 = 3 to bucket 3: [73]. 101 mod 7 = 3 to bucket 3: [73, 101]. Final chains: bucket 0: 700; bucket 1: 50 to 85 to 92; bucket 3: 73 to 101; bucket 6: 76. Buckets 2, 4, 5 empty. Search for 92: hash once, walk the chain — 3 comparisons. No probing, no tombstones.
Slide 13 lays out the two collision strategies side by side. The choice matters for deletion, load factor and cache behaviour. when you expect many collisions or need simple deletion without tombstones. when the table stays small and you want to avoid pointer chasing and memory overhead.
Look at the chaining example on slide 9. Why do you think the slide chose m = 7, a prime, rather than m = 8? What would happen to the distribution of these particular keys if m were 8?

Binary search trees: search, insert and delete.
Slide 3 of your deck defines the vocabulary: a leaf has no children, a subtree is a node plus all its descendants, and the height of a tree is the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path.
Slide 4 adds the core rule: for every node, all keys in the left subtree are smaller, all keys in the right subtree are larger — distinct keys only. That rule is what makes searching possible: at each node you decide left or right, halving the possibilities.
Inserting keys in sorted order (1, 2, 3, …) breaks this advantage: slide 8 warns that it builds a chain of height n minus 1, turning every operation into O of n. You already know from heaps that a balanced shape matters; a BST that stays balanced keeps search, insert and delete at O of log n.
You'll work through search, insert and delete on the BST from slide 4: root 50, left child 30, right child 70, and leaves 20, 40, 60, 80. Keep the tree diagram open — each step changes the tree or tells you where to look. Search for key 60 iteratively. Start at the root (node with key 50).
60 50, so move to the right child (70). 60 70, so move to the left child (60). 60 === 60, stop. Return the node. The loop from slide 5: while (node !== null && key !== node.key) node = key node.key ? node.left : node.right. Search for key 55 (absent key). Start at 50. 55 50 to go to 70. 55 70 to go to 60.
55 60 to go to 60's left child, which is null. The loop exits with node === null. Return null. Insert key 55 into the tree. Slide 5 says: search for the key, then attach a new leaf where the search fell off. Search for 55: 50 to 70 to 60 to null at 60's left. Create a new node with key 55 and set 60.left = that node.
Delete leaf 20. Slide 7: leaf case — just remove it. Find node 20 (50 to 30 to 20). 20 has no children. Set 30.left = null. The node is gone. Delete node 30 (one child — 40). Find node 30. It has one child: 40. Slide 7 says replace the node by its child. Set the parent's (50's) left pointer to 30's child (40).
Now 50.left = 40. Delete root 50 (two children). Slide 7: copy the in-order successor (smallest key in the right subtree) into the node, then delete the successor. The right subtree of 50 is rooted at 70; its smallest key is 60 (70 to 60). Copy 60 into the root (root.key = 60).
Now delete the original 60 node, which has one child (80). Replace 70.left with 60's child (80). Tree root is now 60.
Search, insert and delete all cost O of h; balanced trees keep h = O of log n, sorted insertion makes h = n minus 1. The iterative search loop checks null before key comparison to avoid null reference errors.
Insert creates a new leaf where the search fell off the tree; duplicates are not inserted (distinct keys assumed). Delete a leaf by setting the parent's child pointer to null. Delete a node with one child by replacing the node with its child (update the parent's pointer).
Delete a node with two children by copying the in-order successor's key, then deleting the successor (which has at most one child). In-order traversal of a BST visits keys in sorted order.

Binary heaps, priority queues and heapsort.
Your final is Wednesday 9am, and last year's paper asks you to trace heaps by hand. The good news: a heap is the simplest tree there is, because it lives inside a flat array.
The shape property from slide 4 of Lecture 4 says the tree is complete — every level full except the last, which fills from the left — and that shape is exactly what the array indices encode. The heap property (min-heap: every parent at most its children) is what lets you find the minimum instantly at index 0.
You already traced hash tables bucket by bucket; a heap trace is the same kind of mechanical work, but the rule is even stricter: after every insert or extract-min, the array must still be a complete tree with the heap property.
Two operations do all the work — sift-up for insert (slide 6) and sift-down for extract-min (slide 8). Master those two loops and the whole node is yours. The trap this node exists to prevent: treating build-heap as n inserts.
Slide 10 shows the bottom-up method (Floyd, 1964) that runs in O of n, and the exam's Q3e asks you to explain the difference. You will trace it, then build it, then explain it.
Trace insert and extract-min on the exact arrays from your slides, then run Floyd's build-heap. Do each step on paper; the array after each step is what the exam wants. Insert 2 into [1, 3, 6, 5, 9, 8] (min-heap). Push 2 to the end: index 6. Its parent is index 2 (value 6). 2 6, so swap to [1, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8, 6].
Now at index 2; parent is index 0 (value 1). 2 1, stop. Extract-min from [1, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8, 6]. Save root 1. Pop the last element (6) and put it at index 0 to [6, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8]. Sift down: children of index 0 are 3 and 2; the smaller is 2, swap to [2, 3, 6, 5, 9, 8]. Index 2 has one child, 8; 6 8, stop.
Build a min-heap from [9, 4, 7, 1, 2, 6] bottom-up. n = 6, so start at index ⌊6/2⌋ minus 1 = 2. Sift-down at index 2: children 5 and 6 (values 2 and 6); smaller is 2, swap to [9, 4, 6, 1, 2, 7]. Next index 1: children 3 and 4 (values 1 and 2); smaller is 1, swap to [9, 1, 6, 4, 2, 7].
Next index 0: children 1 and 2 (values 1 and 6); smaller is 1, swap to [1, 9, 6, 4, 2, 7]; sift down again: children of index 1 are 3 and 4 (values 4 and 2); smaller is 2, swap to [1, 2, 6, 4, 9, 7]. Heapsort: build a max-heap, then extract n minus 1 times.
Build a max-heap (same bottom-up, but sift up the larger child). Then repeat n minus 1 times: swap root with the last element, shrink the heap by one, sift-down the new root. Each extraction puts the current maximum at the end, so the array sorts in place.
Slide 10 shows the steps; here is the full working. n = 6, so the first internal node is at index ⌊6/2⌋ minus 1 = 2. i = 2 (value 7): children at 5 and 6 are 2 and 6; smaller is 2 to swap to [9, 4, 6, 1, 2, 7]. i = 1 (value 4): children at 3 and 4 are 1 and 2; smaller is 1 to swap to [9, 1, 6, 4, 2, 7].
i = 0 (value 9): children at 1 and 2 are 1 and 6; smaller is 1 to swap to [1, 9, 6, 4, 2, 7]; now sift down from index 1: children at 3 and 4 are 4 and 2; smaller is 2 to swap to [1, 2, 6, 4, 9, 7]. Final min-heap: [1, 2, 6, 4, 9, 7].
Each parent at most its children: 1 at most 2, 1 at most 6, 2 at most 4, 2 at most 9, 6 at most 7.
The min-heap from slide 7's insert walkthrough, shown as a tree with array indices.
